tldr: A new framework called FORCA enables large language models to interpret wrist force sensor data, autonomously generating real-time control code and refining logic upon failures directly on real hardware. Without demonstrations or prior training, it tackles challenging contact-rich tasks like opening doors and peeling cucumbers with impressive accuracy.
hero_caption: The overall cycle of automatic program refinement in FORCA. Taking cucumber peeling as an example, the agent compares execution outcome images with force logs to diagnose contact loss, then resolves the issue by adding feedback control code that pauses forward motion until the blade makes contact.
overview:
Recently, coding agents that prompt foundation models (LLMs and VLMs) to write Python programs for robot control have attracted significant attention. However, traditional frameworks rely almost exclusively on vision. Vision alone cannot fully capture the exact position of transparent objects, object mass or friction, or subtle changes in contact states as targets move, leading to frequent failures in contact-rich tasks.

To address this, the authors developed FORCA, an agent that leverages wrist force/torque (F/T) sensor measurements. The core idea is to fully exploit force across two time scales: real-time control during execution and program refinement between trials. During execution, it refines position estimates via contact detection and regulates pressing force with high-speed 100 Hz feedback. Between executions, it diagnoses failure causes by cross-referencing recorded force time-series data with camera images, rewriting the control logic itself.

This study uses no demonstration data and no prior simulation training. The framework was evaluated on a real UR5e robot arm across five demanding tasks: opening a transparent drawer, operating a door handle, sliding a block, wiping a vase, and peeling a cucumber. Results demonstrated that FORCA significantly improved task success rates over a vision-only agent and dramatically reduced contact loss in wiping and peeling tasks.
contributions: Proposed a coding agent that directly generates motion planning and force feedback control code utilizing wrist force/torque measurements from language instructions and images.

Introduced a novel refinement mechanism that analyzes robot execution outcomes (visual images and time-series force logs) to iteratively modify force-control conditions and parameters directly on physical hardware.

Achieved high contact precision, physical adaptation, and contact maintenance solely through trial-and-error on real robots, without requiring human demonstrations or reinforcement learning in simulation.

sections.heading: Why Do Robot Coding Agents Need Force Feedback?
sections.summary: Vision-based coding agents struggle with transparent objects and fine force adjustments. FORCA incorporates force sensing into code generation and refinement to achieve contact-rich manipulation.
sections.details:
Coding agents based on large language models excel at composing robot behavior programs from natural language instructions. However, their decision-making has largely relied solely on vision (camera images) and proprioception (such as joint angles).

This creates a major blind spot. In real-world contact tasks, transparent objects or reflective surfaces often cause geometric estimation errors. Furthermore, object mass and friction coefficients cannot be determined from appearance alone. Maintaining consistent contact when targets move or have uneven surfaces, such as during wiping or peeling, is also exceptionally difficult using vision feedback alone.

FORCA was introduced to solve these issues. It embeds force and torque measurements from a wrist F/T sensor into both code generation and refinement. Specifically, it tackles three contact-rich manipulation challenges:
- Precision manipulation: Corrects grasp position offsets mechanically through contact probing.
- Physical adaptation: Grasps changes in object mass and friction from mechanical responses to adjust motion parameters.
- Contact regulation: Maintains a steady pressing force in real time despite surface variations or object motion.

In real-robot experiments across five tasks—including opening drawers, operating door handles, and peeling cucumbers—FORCA demonstrated performance that far surpassed vision-only approaches.

sections.heading: How Does FORCA Differ from Prior Robot Agents?
sections.summary: Prior works attempted to handle force, but they relied on invoking fixed motion primitives or extensive pre-training. FORCA is unique because it writes and rewrites the control logic itself from scratch on the fly.
sections.details:
To understand where this work stands, let us look at three related research lines.

### Foundation-Model-Based Manipulation
Generating robot programs with language models and VLMs is an active area of research, but feedback has centered on vision and language. Earlier studies touching on force either called pre-defined compliant control functions or merely adjusted target force values. No prior agent generated task-specific force feedback control code itself and rewrote the logic based on execution logs like FORCA.

### Contact-Based Perception and Physical Adaptation
Estimating object shape or position via touch and force, as well as identifying latent physical parameters like mass and friction, have long histories. However, these methods required designing dedicated exploration behaviors or aligning with physics simulators. FORCA allows the LLM itself to decide where and how to probe at deployment time, adapting without additional model training.

### Reactive Force-Controlled Manipulation
Impedance control and direct force control using force sensors are classical and powerful approaches. Recently, end-to-end methods incorporating force via imitation learning or reinforcement learning have also grown. However, classical methods require handcrafted threshold tuning, while learning methods demand massive amounts of real-world data or demonstrations. FORCA leverages the strengths of classical control while letting an LLM handle writing controller code and tuning parameters.

sections.heading: How FORCA Works: Writing, Executing, and Refining with Force
sections.summary: FORCA composes task code by assembling initial skill modules. It operates with 100 Hz force feedback during execution, then inspects force logs afterward to repair logic flaws.
sections.details:
The FORCA pipeline consists of three main components.

### III-A Force-Aware Program Generation
The agent is provided with initial skill modules built from open-source tools (SAM 3 for object segmentation, GraspGen for grasp candidate generation, and PyRoKi for trajectory planning). When given an instruction, the agent generates a Python script combining these modules. Crucially, it directly writes code to read wrenches (force and torque vectors) from the wrist F/T sensor, implementing logic such as contact-based approach stopping and velocity corrections based on force errors.

### III-B Contact-Responsive Execution
Once the program runs on the robot, it executes autonomously without querying the foundation model. Two key mechanisms take place:
- Geometric refinement: Before grasping, the gripper gently touches the target (probing), deducing the object's precise height and location from the robot's end-effector pose at the moment of contact.
- Real-time force feedback: During tasks requiring sustained contact, a 100 Hz control loop running on the host PC reads F/T sensor values via RTDE (the real-time data communication interface of UR robots). It updates Cartesian velocity commands based on differences from the target force and quickly pauses forward motion if contact is lost.

### III-C Program Refinement via Execution Feedback
After each rollout, the agent inspects the resulting images along with time-series logs of force and robot states. It can even write small Python scripts to analyze specific time windows in the logs. Once it identifies why a failure occurred, it rewrites not just motion parameters, but also contact detection thresholds and the control logic itself. After passing syntax and reachability safety checks, it proceeds to the next rollout.

The robot acquires tools through a pipeline of (a) tool segmentation using SAM 3, (b) grasp candidate generation with GraspGen and VLM-based selection, (c) collision-free trajectory planning with PyRoKi, and (d) physical picking execution.
captions.F3: A concrete example of program refinement during cucumber peeling. By discovering that an unpeeled section aligned with a sudden drop in force, the agent resolved the failure by adding conditional code that pauses forward progression until force exceeds a threshold.

sections.heading: Real-Robot Experiments: Testing the Power of Force on 5 Tough Tasks
sections.summary: Tested across five tasks: opening a drawer, turning a door handle, sliding a block, wiping a vase, and peeling a cucumber. FORCA achieved dramatically higher success rates and contact maintenance compared to a vision-only agent.
sections.details:
Experiments were conducted using a UR5e arm, a WSG-50 gripper, and a RealSense D455 camera. Claude 3.5 Sonnet served as the coding agent's engine. It was compared against a vision-only agent with access to the same model and basic skills, but blocked from receiving force data.

### IV-B 1 Precision Manipulation (Drawer Opening and Door Handle Turning)
These tasks involved turning a low-tolerance door handle and pulling a transparent drawer knob. Relying only on vision led to large position errors on the transparent acrylic knob, causing grasp failures. FORCA corrected positional errors down to a few millimeters by performing fingertip contact probing. Consequently, over 10 trials, task success soared from 40% to 100% in drawer opening and from 10% to 100% in door handle operation compared to the vision-only baseline.

### IV-B 2 Physical Property Adaptation (Cube-to-Target)
This task required nudging a block so it slides and stops inside a designated target area. The friction and restitution dynamics varied drastically by swapping object mass (a 61.9 g cube vs. a 663.6 g metal cylinder) and floor surfaces (a whiteboard vs. a wooden board). Starting from code completed in one environment, FORCA adjusted impulse and strike velocity parameters in just a few additional trials, reaching the target area with significantly fewer trials than developing from scratch.

### IV-B 3 Online Contact Regulation (Vase Wiping and Cucumber Peeling)
These tasks evaluated erasing marker lines on a curved vase and peeling a cucumber held in a human hand. For vase wiping, code tuned on a stationary vase was deployed zero-shot to a dynamic setting where a person moved the vase. The vision-only approach failed to follow the moving vase, suffering a 55.9% contact loss rate and leaving 87% of the marker intact (13% removal). FORCA maintained steady contact force via its 100 Hz loop, achieving a contact loss rate of only 0.5% and a 93% removal rate. In cucumber peeling, FORCA kept the blade firmly engaged without applying excessive force (above 10 N), yielding long, continuous peelings.

### IV-C & IV-D Development Cost and Refinement Analysis
Regarding iteration overhead during development, robot execution took 1 to 3 minutes, whereas agent reasoning and inference took 4 to 10 minutes. Detailed analysis of the door handle task confirmed that FORCA performed high-quality logic revisions based on force data, such as detecting the latch release when hitting the mechanical stop (indicated by a sharp force spike).

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Horizons for FORCA
sections.summary: Key challenges moving forward include long trial-and-error turnaround times, the limited spatial resolution of wrist sensors, and reasoning difficulty in complex, multi-stage tasks.
sections.details:
The authors identify three limitations to address for practical deployment:

- Cost of iterative rollouts: Each refinement cycle takes several to 10 minutes, with most of that time spent on LLM inference. Because failures occur directly on real hardware, streamlining the process—such as performing initial refinement in simulation before moving to the real robot—is desirable.
- Sensing limits of force feedback: The current system relies solely on a wrist 6-axis F/T sensor. While it measures resultant forces on the wrist, it cannot resolve force distributions across individual fingertips. Integrating fingertip tactile arrays could extend capabilities to more delicate tasks.
- Task complexity: In tasks with very long horizons or extremely tight force constraints, identifying the exact root cause of failure becomes difficult, and the agent may fail to converge within the allowed budget of 20 iterations.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Code That Evolves by Conversing with the Physical World
sections.summary: FORCA is a framework that autonomously writes and revises code with force feedback. Adapting to environments without demonstrations, it opens a new avenue for stabilizing real-world contact manipulation.
sections.details:
FORCA introduces a new manipulation paradigm where robots refine their own code through force feedback while working on site. Updating control logic directly from trial-and-error logs without pre-training or human teaching is particularly powerful for dynamic environments like homes and factories.

In the future, reusing accumulated code libraries and integrating imitation learning or Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models as low-level sub-skills could unlock even more complex and flexible autonomous operations.

takeaways: Force sensing is indispensable alongside vision for contact-rich tasks, and LLMs can effectively infer failure causes (such as contact loss or mechanical limits) from wrist F/T sensor time-series logs.
Decoupling the architecture into two stages—generating fast real-time force control code and revising logic through post-trial failure diagnosis—is highly effective.
When physical properties like mass or friction change, taking existing working control code as a starting point allows rapid adaptation in just a few real-robot trials.

Advanced contact tasks can be solved without collecting large demonstration datasets or building complex simulators, relying entirely on foundation-model-driven self-refinement loops at deployment time.
limitations: Each program refinement cycle requires 4 to 10 minutes of LLM inference time and multiple real-robot trials, incurring notable time and physical safety costs.
Relying on a single wrist 6-axis force/torque sensor limits the ability to perceive multi-finger contact locations or localized tactile states.
For tasks with long sequential horizons or overly complex force constraints, the LLM may fail to accurately diagnose failure causes, potentially exhausting the maximum iteration budget.
